verdict.rationale: The cited corpus attests both a free pole and an ordered pole within the same Pauline material and ranks neither into a single mandated form, so the proposition that both are defensible across a wide spectrum is supported while any one form is underdetermined. The grammar is decisive on this point. In 1 Corinthians 14:26 the present active indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) verb "has" (echei, G2192), repeated for each item, describes that "each one" (ekastos, G1538) actually has a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation, and the present middle imperative (a command in ongoing, middle-voice form) "let it be done" (ginestho, G1096) caps it with "let all things be done toward building up" (panta pros oikodomen). The identical imperative "let it be done" (ginestho) governs 1 Corinthians 14:40, "let all things be done decently and in order" (panta euschemonos kai kata taxin). One verb thus binds freedom and order together and forecloses neither. The word for "order" (taxis, G5010) is itself two-sensed across the canon, plain orderliness in 1 Corinthians 14:40 and Colossians 2:5 but a fixed appointed arrangement in Luke 1:8 and the Melchizedek order of Hebrews, so the word cannot by itself mandate a set liturgy (a fixed script for the gathering). Set elements are nonetheless present, the articular (with the article "the") "Amen" (amen, G0281) presupposed in 1 Corinthians 14:16, the articular triad "the reading, the exhortation, the teaching" (te anagnosei, te paraklesei, te didaskalia) in 1 Timothy 4:13, and "psalm" (psalmos, G5568) which itself names both the inherited Psalter and a brought song. Because the vocabulary co-attests fixed and free without ranking them, the verdict is disputed.

scripture.force: The morphology (word-form analysis) is load-bearing here. "Each one" (ekastos, G1538, nominative singular, the subject form meaning each one) is the subject, and "has" (echei, G2192) is present active indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) third singular, repeated once per item, so the verse describes what is actually the case when the assembly gathers, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. The clause closes with "let all things be done toward building up" (panta pros oikodomen ginestho), where "let it be done" (ginestho, G1096) is present middle imperative (an ongoing command in middle voice) third singular, let all things be done toward "building up" (oikodome, G3619). The distributive subject (a subject that spreads action across many people, one by one) plus the open inventory of contributions warrants participatory and varied worship, while the governing imperative subordinates that freedom to edification (building one another up) rather than to any named script.

"But let all things be done decently and according to order" (panta de euschemonos kai kata taxin ginestho) closes the chapter that authorized open contribution with the SAME present middle imperative (ongoing command in middle voice) "let it be done" (ginestho, G1096) used in verse 26, now constrained by "decently" (euschemonos, G2156, adverb meaning decently or becomingly) and "according to order" (kata taxin, G5010). The single repeated imperative is what binds the free pole and the order pole together. "Order" (taxis) is two-sensed across the canon, plain orderliness in this verse and in Colossians 2:5 but a fixed appointed arrangement in Luke 1:8 (priestly course) and the Melchizedek order of Hebrews, so the word warrants structure without by itself mandating a set liturgy (a fixed script for the gathering).

Mutual "teaching" (didaskontes) and "admonishing" (nouthetountes, from noutheteo, G3560), both present active participles (ongoing verbal adjectives), in "psalms, hymns, spiritual songs" (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais), three juxtaposed dative (in the "to or with" grammatical case) nouns with no copula (the linking verb "is") or ranking between them. The adjective "spiritual" (pneumatikais, G4152) agrees grammatically only with the feminine "songs" (odais), so the text does not force whether all three are fixed categories or one loose threefold description. "Psalm" (psalmos, G5568) itself names both the inherited Psalter (its sense in Luke 20:42 and Acts 1:20) and a brought congregational song, so a single word holds both inherited and free. The participle "singing" (adontes, from ado, G0103) is governed by the imperative "let dwell" (enoiketo), let the word of Christ dwell richly. The verse supports breadth of song form rather than one mandated mode.

"Give attention to" (prosechē, G4337, present active imperative (ongoing command) second singular) governs three articular (with the article "the") datives ("to or with" forms), "the reading" (tē anagnōsei), "the exhortation" (tē paraklēsei), "the teaching" (tē didaskalia), that is the public reading (anagnosis, G0320, used elsewhere only of public or Scripture reading), the exhortation (paraklesis, G3874), the teaching (didaskalia, G1319). The repeated definite article designates recurring, assignable elements of the gathering, the closest the cited corpus comes to a fixed order of service, and grounds the set-form pole. The verse is a charge to one overseer, so the words do not state whether the triad is a closed script binding every assembly.

The phrase "the Amen" (to Amen, G0281) is articular (with the article "the"), the recognized fixed congregational response that someone is expected to say at the giving of thanks (eucharistia, the thanksgiving). Paul presupposes this set word as a known element of the gathering rather than introducing it, which is a concrete instance of an inherited fixed form embedded in the same chapter that authorizes open each-one contribution, so it stands alongside verse 26 rather than against it.

complicating_texts.resolution: The order rule "decently and according to order" (euschemonos kai kata taxin) sits in the same chapter as the open "each one" (ekastos) contribution of 1 Corinthians 14:26 and could be read as canceling spontaneity. It is resolved as a regulating constraint rather than a competing form, because the very same present middle imperative (ongoing command in middle voice) "let it be done" (ginestho) governs both verses, so order describes HOW the varied contributions proceed and does not forbid them. "Order" (taxis) carries a fixed-arrangement sense elsewhere (Luke 1:8, Hebrews on Melchizedek), but its sense in 1 Corinthians 14:40 parallels Colossians 2:5 plain orderliness, so it cannot be pressed into a mandated liturgy (a fixed script for the gathering). Both poles therefore stand together and the verdict is disputed rather than tilted to set forms.

The articular (with the article "the") triad of reading, exhortation, and teaching could be read as a fixed mandated liturgy (a required script) that excludes free contribution. It is resolved as a designation of recurring elements within Timothy's pastoral charge (the imperative "give attention to" (prosechē) is second singular, addressed to one overseer), not a closed script binding every assembly, so it warrants structure without ruling out the participatory pattern of 1 Corinthians 14:26.

The articular (with the article "the") "Amen" could be read as proof that worship is fundamentally fixed and formulaic, overriding the each-one freedom of verse 26. It is resolved as one inherited set element presupposed within an otherwise participatory gathering, which is precisely why the chapter co-attests both, a known fixed response word AND open varied contribution, leaving the overall form underdetermined rather than settling it toward liturgy.

variants.note: The cited verses lie outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM (a computer-assisted method for tracing manuscript relationships) was not consulted (not_in_ecm_scope, meaning outside the scope of the critical edition of New Testament textual variants). The text-critical marks carried in the bundle for 1 Corinthians 14:26, Colossians 3:16, and 1 Timothy 4:13 touch word order and minor lexical choice (for example the editorial sigla, that is, scholarly marker symbols, on "each one" (ekastos), "revelation" (apokalypsin), and the song nouns) and do not bear on the order versus freedom question, so the verdict is variant robust.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that admits in worship only what Scripture positively warrants finds explicit lexical warrant for public reading, exhortation, teaching (1 Timothy 4:13), congregational song (Colossians 3:16), and the fixed "Amen" (amen) response (1 Corinthians 14:16), and treats "decently and according to order" (euschemonos kai kata taxin) as the controlling rule. In its strongest form this lens reads the articular (with the article "the") triad and the set "Amen" as evidence that the gathering already carried inherited fixed elements, favoring ordered forms, while still conceding that the breadth of psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs leaves the precise shape open.

A reading that permits whatever Scripture does not forbid leans on the present indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) "has" (echei) and the distributive "each one" (ekastos) in 1 Corinthians 14:26, plus the unranked, copula-free (lacking the linking verb "is") song triad of Colossians 3:16, to license spontaneous and varied contribution as the actual described shape of the assembly. In its strongest form this lens notes that the only imperative attached is "let it be done toward building up" (ginestho pros oikodomen), not a command to adopt any set script, so freedom is the warranted default, bounded only by edification and order, which yields the same wide spectrum from the other direction.

A reading that takes the proposition on its own terms, that both set and free worship are defensible if what is done has scriptural warrant, finds the strongest support, because the canon supplies BOTH patterns in one chapter and never ranks them. The single repeated imperative "let it be done" (ginestho) and the two-sensed "order" (taxis) are exactly the lexical features that keep either pole from being made the exclusive rule, so the spectrum claim is the reading the words best sustain.

hermeneutics.notes: All three interpretive lenses land on or inside a spectrum rather than a single mandated form, which is why the lexical witness is recorded as disputed. The two-pole material is co-attested in the same Pauline chapter (1 Corinthians 14) and is reinforced, not resolved, by Colossians 3:16 and 1 Timothy 4:13.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What forms may a gathered assembly use in corporate worship, and does the cited corpus mandate one form, permit a range, or leave the matter open.
stem_audit.notes: The stem pairs liturgical with set forms and spontaneous with Spirit-led, and the Spirit-led label preloads the conclusion that unscripted worship is the work of the Spirit, which is a contested framing the words do not establish. The phrases biblically defensible and scriptural warrant also gesture toward a regulative posture. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form strips the loaded labels so the lexical question is simply which forms the words warrant. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, verdict unchanged from the prior file: disputed.

lay_summary: This question asks whether Scripture mandates one form of corporate worship or allows a range, from set written forms to free Spirit prompted participation. The cited Greek words pull in two directions at once, and the grammar is the key. In 1 Corinthians 14:26 the word "each one" (ekastos) is the subject, and the verb "has" (echei) is a present tense form that simply describes what is the case when believers gather, each one has a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation. That open list, with no command to adopt any script, supports varied participatory worship. The verse ends with a command, "let all things be done toward building up" (ginestho pros oikodomen), and a few lines later the very same command verb returns in 1 Corinthians 14:40, "let all things be done decently and in order" (euschemonos kai kata taxin). One verb "let it be done" (ginestho) governs both the freedom and the order, so neither cancels the other. The word for "order" (taxis) is itself two-sided across the Bible, it means plain tidiness here but a fixed appointed arrangement elsewhere, like a priest serving in his appointed course, so the word alone cannot prove that a set liturgy (a fixed script for the gathering) is required. At the same time fixed elements are clearly present. The same chapter assumes "the Amen" (amen) as a known set response, First Timothy 4:13 lists three regular activities each marked with the word "the", the reading, the exhortation, the teaching, and the word "psalm" (psalmos) names both the inherited book of Psalms and a freshly brought song. Colossians 3:16 lists "psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs" (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais) side by side with nothing ranking them. Because the words hold fixed and free together and never put one above the other, the evidence does not single out one required form. It supports the claim that a wide spectrum can carry scriptural warrant while leaving any single form undecided, which is why the verdict is recorded as disputed rather than a plain yes or no.
